why: Ruvyxa resolves every import twice. crates/ruvyxa_bundler/src/resolver.rs
walks the graph for `ruvyxa build`; packages/ruvyxa/runtime/compiler.mjs
walks it again for the dev server, the prerender workers, and every
function artifact an adapter assembles. A specifier the two answer
differently is not a build error — it is a bundle that runs different code
than the one the build reported.
They did answer differently. compiler.mjs used createRequire().resolve(),
which is Node's CommonJS resolver and matches only the conditions
["node", "require"]. For any dual package the Rust client bundler took
browser/import while the JavaScript graph inlined the require build into
the same browser bundle, and an edge function artifact never saw `worker`
or `edge-light` at all.
`exportsJson` holds the exports field as source text rather than as parsed
JSON, because condition order is load-bearing and a JSON object read into
a sorted map would lose it. Both hosts parse the text themselves.
Two departures from Node are deliberate and are asserted here rather than
described in a comment: `require` is a second pass instead of a peer of
`import` (Node takes the first supported condition in author order, which
hands CommonJS to a bundler that emits ESM), and a subpath the map does
not cover falls through to the legacy fields instead of failing, with only
an explicit null blocking.
Two behaviours here are asserted because both hosts share them rather than
because Node agrees. A star that expands to nothing produces a target that
does not exist on disk, so the probe fails harmlessly rather than being
refused up front. And a subpath is matched against the map alone: neither
host implements Node's separate refusal of a specifier ending in `/`.
`result` is the ordered list of package-relative targets, or the string
"blocked" for an explicit null, or "unmatched" when the map answers
nothing and the legacy fields take over. Existence on disk is not part of
this table: each host probes the file system its own way.
`react-server` is a bundle target rather than a flag, because the condition
changes which *file* a specifier names: React itself resolves to a build
with no useState in it. Ordering it ahead of `node` is what makes a package
that ships both reach its server-components build — the last case here is
react-server-dom-webpack's own exports map, which returns a stub that
refuses to load unless the condition is on.
`fileProbe` is the other half of resolution: once a specifier names a path,
which file on disk that path stands for. Both hosts probe in one order —
the TypeScript source a written extension stands for, the exact path, an
appended extension, a directory index — and both had the same defect at
opposite ends. The Rust probe substituted the last dotted segment for every
candidate, so `./util.inspect` asked for `util.js` and never for
`util.inspect.js`, the file `object-inspect` ships and the one Node finds;
`resolvePackageRelative` in compiler.mjs substituted the same way for a
package entry. A dot inside a basename is ordinary, and Node appends.
`files` are created empty under a temporary directory, `specifier` is
resolved against it, and `expect` is the file that must answer or null.
`resolutionOrder` is the step before either of those: which *source* a
non-relative specifier is looked up in, and in what order. Every other
section here describes a rule that applies once a package has been chosen;
nothing described the walk that chooses it, and the two hosts had drifted
apart exactly there. resolver.rs probed the project root with the bare
specifier between `tsconfig` and `node_modules`, so `import 'utils'` took
<root>/utils/index.ts for the client bundle while compiler.mjs — which has
no such step — took node_modules/utils for the dev server and every
prerender worker. One import, two files, no diagnostic from either host.
The order both hosts now hold is the one Node and `tsc` already agree on:
`tsconfig` `paths`, then `tsconfig` `baseUrl`, then `node_modules`. There
is no project-root step. A bare specifier names a package; a project file
is reached with a relative import, or by declaring `baseUrl` — which is
root-relative resolution asked for out loud, and which both hosts honour.
Deleting the step could have broken a project that relied on it silently:
the specifier would become an unresolved external, which no host reports
and every host fails at run time. So the drop is loud instead. When a bare
specifier resolves to nothing anywhere and a file at the project root
would have answered it, both hosts refuse the build with RUV1808 naming
that file. Note that `tsc` was already refusing these imports; the probe
made the bundler disagree with the type checker, not just with itself.
A case with `absolute: true` has the temporary project root prefixed onto
its specifier, with forward slashes — the form a generated entry emits.
That case is here because on Windows such a path carries a drive prefix
and no leading slash, so resolver.rs did not recognise it as absolute and
only the project-root probe was answering it. Removing the probe with no
case for this shape broke every generated entry on Windows at once. It
sits in a project with no tsconfig deliberately: a `baseUrl` joined with
an absolute path yields that path, so a project that has one answers this
specifier whether or not the branch above recognises it.
That case states the rule; it is not by itself a gate for the Windows bug.
With the drive-prefix branch removed it still passes, because the package
walk splits `C:/x/app/page.ts` into a package named `C:` and joins the
rest onto it, and Windows reads `C:` plus a relative path as drive-
relative — which lands back on the same file whenever the project is on
drive C. `cargo run -p ruvyxa_cli -- build --root examples/demo` is what
actually fails, immediately and on the first route.
The `imports` section covers Node's `#` specifiers, which neither graph
implemented. `packageNameAndExportKey` read `#internal/db` as a package named
`#internal` with the key `./db`, that matched nothing, and the specifier reached
the "unknown bare specifier is external" branch — so a client bundle carried a
hoisted `import … from "#dep"` with no build error at all and the browser failed
to load the module. Both halves now answer a `#` key through the same subpath
matcher `exports` uses, and this table is what keeps them saying the same thing.

exports.name: author order decides between conditions that compete
require is a second pass even when the author writes it first
a package that ships only CommonJS still resolves off the edge target
node wins for ssr and is invisible to the browser
worker and edge-light are the edge target's own conditions
edge-light answers when worker is absent
an explicit null blocks the subpath outright
a subpath the map does not cover is unmatched, not blocked
a bare condition map answers only the root key
a string exports field answers only the root key
a string exports field does not answer a subpath
an array offers its entries in order
a target that is not package-relative is not a target
nested condition objects are walked
a wildcard subpath substitutes every star in the target
the longest matching prefix wins over a catch-all star
a longer suffix breaks a prefix tie
an exact subpath beats a wildcard that also matches
a star may expand to nothing, and the path it builds simply is not there
a pattern with two stars is not a pattern
an unknown condition is skipped rather than taken
a condition map with no supported condition is unmatched
module competes inside the first pass, ahead of require
react-server wins over node for a package that ships both
author order still decides when react-server is written last
exports.$why: Node matches conditions in the order the author wrote them, and both `node` and `react-server` are accepted here, so the first one wins. This is deliberately NOT a second departure like the `require` pass: that one exists because this bundler emits ESM and a CommonJS build cannot be a peer of an ESM one, which is a property of the output. Here both builds load, and which is right is the package author's call — the packages that mean it, React's own among them, list `react-server` first.

exports.name: a package with no react-server build falls back to its node build
react-server is invisible to every other target
the react-server binding of react-server-dom-webpack, as shipped

legacyEntries.name: browser competes only for a browser bundle
module is preferred to main on every target
a package with no entry fields falls back to the directory layout
a subpath is taken literally and the fields do not apply
the object form of browser names no entry point

fileProbe.name: a basename with a dot is appended to, not replaced
appending beats replacing when both files exist
a minified basename keeps both dots
a written .js names the TypeScript source it stands for
a written .js answers itself when no source is beside it
an exact file wins over an appended one
a .cjs file is found by appending
a directory index is the last resort
nothing answers a specifier with no file behind it

resolutionOrder.name: a bare specifier names a package, never a project directory

cases.name: an installed package wins over a project directory of the same name
an installed package with no project directory beside it resolves
a tsconfig paths alias wins over both the package and the directory
a project directory no package answers is refused, not dropped
a project file at the root is refused the same way
a bare specifier nothing anywhere answers stays external

resolutionOrder.name: baseUrl is how a project asks for root-relative resolution

cases.name: baseUrl answers before node_modules, exactly as tsc resolves it
baseUrl reaches a nested project file a bare specifier cannot

resolutionOrder.name: a generated entry names an absolute path, with no tsconfig in the project

cases.name: an absolute path is answered as a path, not as a package
a bare specifier a project directory shadows is still refused

imports.name: an exact key answers the specifier that spells it
conditions inside an imports target read exactly as they do in exports
one `*` substitutes into the target, the same wildcard grammar exports uses
the longest matching prefix wins, so `#f/*` never shadows `#f/deep/*`
a key the map does not declare is unmatched, not guessed at
null takes the specifier away, exactly as it does in exports
a bare target is left unresolved rather than followed into another package
